values: the same fields, when a device goes away

headers.title: BNeuralSession
headers.text: A model loaded onto a device and ready to run.

items.name: BNeuralSession
items.text: Setting a session up is the slow part: the device's back end translates the network and uploads its weights. Running it is fast and can be repeated as often as needed. When a session is set up, the kit asks the back end which operators the device can run, splits the network into stretches for the device and stretches for the CPU, and has the back end make a program for each of its stretches. A run the device fails is done by the CPU; a device that goes away, or fails three runs in a row, loses its stretches to the CPU for good. A session therefore always works and gives the same answers. The input and output tensors belong to the session and keep their memory between runs. A session runs one thing at a time; several sessions, including sessions of the same model, can run at once and share a device.

headers.title: BSpeechRecognizer
headers.text: Speech to text on the machine itself, with a Whisper model the kit runs. Nothing leaves the machine.

items.name: BSpeechRecognizer
items.text: Audio goes in as it is recorded, in any raw format of the Media Kit; text comes out as messages, and the caller never waits for the model. The recognizer has its own thread, which does the work. Its methods may be called from any thread, and deleting it is safe at any time: it waits for the step the model is in (at most one encoder run). Whisper works on 30-second windows and marks where phrases end; a phrase is final when the model has seen its end.

headers.title: Operators
headers.text: The operators a network is made of, whatever file it came from. They follow TensorFlow Lite's, whose quantized arithmetic is specified to the bit; the CPU kernels reproduce it, which makes the CPU device the reference every back end is checked against. Each operator has a fixed list of inputs and, where noted, a parameter structure. An input index of −1 means "not given" (a convolution without bias). `neural_operator_name()` and `neural_operator_params_size()` describe a code.

items.name: neural_operator_code
items.text: Inputs, then the parameter structure.
values: input; converts between types and quantizations
box encodings `[1, anchors, 4]`, class scores `[1, anchors, classes]`, anchors (constant). Outputs boxes `[1, n, 4]` (top, left, bottom, right), classes, scores, count; `neural_detection_params`
a, b: `[…, m, k] × […, k, n]`, leading dimensions broadcast; `neural_batch_matmul_params`
input, indices (int32 or int64): slices along one dimension (embeddings); an index out of range fails the run; `neural_gather_params`

no padding: only positions where the whole window fits

headers.title: The back-end API
headers.text: For people adding hardware. A back end is an add-on in `add-ons/neural` that makes one kind of hardware usable: it finds its devices (usually through the kernel driver's nodes under `/dev/npu`), says which operators a device can run, and turns stretches of such operators into programs. The kit does the rest. See [Writing a back end](docs/neural/#backends) and [the example back end](docs/neural/examples/#backend).

items.text: One per add-on, made by `instantiate_neural_backend()`, living as long as the team's roster. It must be thread safe: programs of different sessions run at the same time.

values: `operators`/`operator_count`: operators that follow one another; `inputs`: tensors they need from outside (constants are not listed); `outputs`: tensors they make that are needed outside
`id` (unique in the back end, stable: `"0"`), `name`, `vendor`, `kind`, `flags`, `priority` (100 for the device that is the reason the machine has an NPU, 50 for a general-purpose GPU)
the one function an add-on exports; return `NULL` when the back end cannot work on this machine
